quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on the vocabulary of crepe, spot and honeycomb weaves: sateen bases, added marks, superimposing and cellular cloth.

questions.q: What does a crepe weave look like on the cloth?
questions.explain: A crepe hides any direction: its marks are scattered so the surface reads as an even pebble. A clear diagonal is the look of a twill and a smooth lustre that of satin.

questions.q: Which is the classic way, from the lecture, of constructing a crepe weave?
options: Alternating plain weave and 2/2 twill in stripes
Lengthening the floats of a satin
Starting with a sateen base and adding one or more marks to every base mark, or superimposing two sateens
Reversing the draft of a twill
questions.explain: The sateen gives a well-scattered skeleton of single marks; the added or superimposed marks thicken it into a pebbled texture without creating lines.

questions.q: A well-made crepe weave shows a visible twill diagonal.
questions.explain: The whole point of building on a sateen base is that the marks are scattered with no two touching, so no diagonal appears; a visible line means the arrangement has failed.

questions.q: In this lecture, what is meant by a 'sateen base'?
options: A sateen repeat with one mark per end that acts as the skeleton to which further marks are added
A sateen woven as the back cloth of a double cloth
questions.explain: The base is the ordinary sateen itself (for example the 8-end sateen): each of its single marks is the anchor for the extra marks that make the crepe.

questions.q: What does 'superimposing' two sateens mean?
options: Placing the marks of one sateen over the marks of another on the same design paper so both sets of lifts combine in one weave
Weaving one above the other as a double cloth
questions.explain: The two sateens are drawn on one repeat and their marks combined; the lecture's 4-end and 6-end sateens superimposed on 12 × 12 is the example.

questions.q: The honeycomb weave is produced by:
options: A straight draft and a sateen lifting plan
A pointed draft and a pointed lifting plan
questions.explain: The draft turns back on itself (1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2) and the lifting plan does the same, and the two together form the diamond cells.

questions.q: In a honeycomb cell, the ridges and the hollows are respectively:
options: Tightly interlaced areas and long floats
Long floats and tightly interlaced areas
questions.explain: The ridges stand up because they are long floats; the hollows are bound tightly and sink. The reverse order is the usual slip.

questions.q: Why is honeycomb a towelling weave?
options: Because its cellular structure of ridges and hollows traps water
Because it is warp-faced and lustrous
Because it is the strongest weave
questions.explain: The diamond cells hold water in their hollows and the floats give a soft, absorbent surface, which is why the weave is used for towels.

questions.q: The 16-end honeycomb is a different weave from the 8-end ordinary honeycomb.
questions.explain: The lecture states that the 16-end version is the same ordinary honeycomb built on a larger cell: the draft and lifting plan are simply pointed over 16 ends instead of 8.

questions.q: Why is the irregular 6-end sateen called irregular?
options: Because 6 has no valid move number, so its single marks must be placed by hand rather than by a fixed move
Because it has two marks per end
questions.explain: Every candidate move for 6 either shares a factor with it (2, 3, 4) or gives a twill (1, 5), so the six marks are arranged irregularly, as with the 4-end satinette.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Repeat sizes when sateens are combined, marks per end, healds for pointed drafts and what changes as a honeycomb cell grows.

questions.q: A 4-end sateen and a 6-end sateen are superimposed. On what repeat must the design be drawn?
questions.explain: The repeat must hold a whole number of each: the lowest common multiple of 4 and 6 is 12. Adding (10) or multiplying (24) the repeats is the usual error.

questions.q: An 8-end sateen derivative has a 4-end satinette superimposed on it. The repeat of the result is:
questions.explain: 4 divides 8, so the satinette fits twice across and twice up the 8 × 8 repeat and the combined weave still repeats on 8 ends × 8 picks.

questions.q: How many marks does an 8-end sateen base carry in one repeat before anything is added?
questions.explain: A sateen has exactly one lift per end (and per pick), so an 8 × 8 base has 8 marks: one eighth of the squares.

questions.q: Two marks are added to every base mark of an 8-end sateen. How many marks does each end now carry?
questions.explain: Each end had its one base mark; adding two to it gives 3 marks per end, so the whole repeat holds 8 × 3 = 24 marks.

questions.q: The 8-end honeycomb is threaded 1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2. How many healds does it need?
questions.explain: The highest heald number in the threading is 5. Ends 6, 7 and 8 come back down healds 4, 3 and 2, so 8 ends share 5 frames.

questions.q: For a pointed draft over n ends of this honeycomb type, the number of healds is:
questions.explain: The draft climbs to the turning heald and comes back without repeating it: 8 ends need 8 ÷ 2 + 1 = 5 healds, 16 ends need 9.

questions.q: In the honeycomb the lifting plan is pointed as well as the draft.
questions.explain: The lecture's honeycomb uses a pointed draft and a pointed lifting plan; it is the combination of the two reversals that closes the diamond cell.

questions.q: Going from the 8-end to the 16-end honeycomb, what changes?
options: The cell becomes larger and the floats longer; it is still the ordinary honeycomb
questions.explain: A larger pointed repeat gives a bigger diamond with longer ridge floats and deeper hollows; healds rise from 5 to 9, not fall.

questions.q: What fraction of the face of a plain 8-end sateen base is covered by warp?
questions.explain: One lift per end in 8 picks: 1 ÷ 8 = 12.5 % warp. 87.5 % would be the 7/1 satin, its back.

questions.q: If marks are added to a sateen base in the same direction on every base mark, the risk is:
options: The marks join into a faint twill line and the crepe loses its non-directional look
questions.explain: Added marks that always extend the same way lengthen the base marks into short diagonals. The arrangement must keep the marks scattered or superimpose a second sateen to break the line.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting marks, percentages, healds and repeats on the point paper of the lecture's crepe and honeycomb designs.

questions.q: An 8-end sateen base has two marks added to every base mark. How many squares are filled in the 8 × 8 repeat?
questions.explain: 8 base marks, each now a group of 3: 8 × 3 = 24 filled squares out of 64.

questions.q: What percentage of the 8 × 8 repeat is filled when an 8-end sateen base carries three marks per end? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: 24 filled squares ÷ 64 = 0.375, i.e. 37.5 % of the face is warp.

questions.q: In the irregular 6-end sateen each end is lifted once. What percentage of the face is warp? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: One lift in 6 picks: 1 ÷ 6 = 0.1667, so 16.7 % warp and 83.3 % weft on the face.

questions.q: How many healds does the 16-end honeycomb need with its pointed draft?
questions.explain: The draft runs 1 2 … 8 9 8 … 2: the turning heald is 9, so 16 ÷ 2 + 1 = 9 healds.

questions.q: A 4-end satinette and a 6-end sateen are superimposed on a 12 × 12 repeat. How many times does the 4-end satinette appear within the repeat?
questions.explain: It fits 12 ÷ 4 = 3 times across and 3 times up: 3 × 3 = 9 copies, contributing 9 × 4 = 36 marks.

questions.q: In the same 12 × 12 superimposition, how many marks does the 6-end sateen contribute?
questions.explain: 2 copies across × 2 up = 4 copies, each with 6 single marks: 4 × 6 = 24 marks (some may coincide with satinette marks).

questions.q: In the honeycomb threading 1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2, how many healds carry two ends per repeat?
questions.explain: Healds 2, 3 and 4 each appear twice (on the way up and on the way down); healds 1 and 5 carry one end each. 3 of the 5 healds carry two ends.

questions.q: An 8-end sateen base uses move 3 and pick 1 lifts end 1. Which end does pick 4 lift?
questions.explain: Pick 2: end 4; pick 3: end 7; pick 4: 10 − 8 = end 2. The base marks therefore sit on ends 1, 4, 7, 2, 5, 8, 3, 6 for picks 1 to 8.

questions.q: If only ONE mark were added to every base mark of an 8-end sateen, what percentage of the repeat would be filled?
questions.explain: 8 ends × 2 marks = 16 of 64 squares = 25 %. The lecture's two-added-marks design gives 37.5 %.

questions.q: The 16-end honeycomb draft climbs 1 to 9 and returns to 2. How many ends does one repeat of the threading contain?
questions.explain: Up: 1 to 9 is 9 ends; down: 8 to 2 is 7 ends; 9 + 7 = 16. Counting the return as 8 ends (repeating heald 9 or 1) gives the wrong 17 or 18.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Choosing crepes and honeycombs for real orders, fitting them to the looms in the shed and curing designs that have gone wrong.

questions.q: A buyer wants a dress fabric with an even, pebbled surface and no visible direction. Which construction do you propose?
options: A crepe built on a sateen base
questions.explain: The sateen-based crepe gives exactly the all-over, non-directional pebble. Twills show a diagonal and satin a smooth lustre.

questions.q: A towel mill wants an absorbent cellular cloth that can be woven on a dobby loom without terry pile. Which weave?
questions.explain: Honeycomb's ridges and hollows trap water, and its pointed draft runs on 5 or 9 healds, well within a dobby. Satin and plain do not form cells.

questions.q: A designer's new crepe shows a faint diagonal across the sample. What is the likely cause and cure?
options: The repeat is too large; halve it
The added marks extend the base marks in one direction and join into a line; rearrange them or superimpose a second sateen
The yarn is too fine; use a coarser count
The reed is too coarse; change the reed
questions.explain: A crepe is only non-directional while its marks stay scattered. Marks that always run the same way from each base mark rebuild a twill. Breaking the arrangement removes the line.

questions.q: A loom in the shed has 8 heald frames. Can it weave the 16-end honeycomb?
options: No: the pointed draft 1 to 9 and back needs 9 healds, so offer the 8-end honeycomb (5 healds) instead
Yes, if the picks are halved
Yes, 16 ends on 8 frames with two ends per heald
questions.explain: 16 ÷ 2 + 1 = 9 healds are needed. The 8-end version on 5 healds gives the same ordinary honeycomb with a smaller cell.

questions.q: Can the 8-end honeycomb run on a tappet loom with 6 frames and an 8-pick limit?
options: Yes: 5 healds and an 8-pick repeat are within both limits
questions.explain: The threading 1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2 uses 5 frames and the lifting plan repeats on 8 picks, so a tappet can weave it.

questions.q: A customer likes the honeycomb towel but wants visibly bigger cells. What do you change?
options: Use the 16-end honeycomb, pointed over more ends
questions.explain: Cell size is set by the length of the pointed repeat: 16 ends gives a larger diamond than 8. Reed or pick changes alter density, not the cell geometry.

questions.q: You are asked to draw a crepe by superimposing a 4-end satinette on a 6-end sateen. What size of design paper repeat do you rule?
questions.explain: The repeat is the lowest common multiple of 4 and 6, which is 12, exactly as the lecture's 12 × 12 design.

questions.q: Because its ridges are long floats, a honeycomb cloth is softer and more absorbent than a plain weave of the same yarn, but less firm.
questions.explain: Long floats lie loose on the surface and soak up water, which suits towels, but they also make the cloth less firm and easier to snag than plain weave.

questions.q: Superimposing the 4-end satinette on the 8-end sateen derivative keeps the repeat at 8 picks. Why does that matter in the mill?
options: The dobby pegging stays 8 picks long, so the existing lifting plan length and tappets can still be used
questions.explain: The 4-end satinette divides exactly into 8, so no longer peg plan is needed; a 6-end addition would have forced a 24-pick repeat.

questions.q: A designer places spots on a plain ground in straight rows and columns. What will the cloth look like, and what is the better arrangement?
options: The spots will disappear; use larger spots
The spots will line up as stripes; distribute them in sateen order so no two are in line
It will look like a crepe; no change needed
questions.explain: Spots in rows read as lines, not as an all-over effect. Placing them on a sateen base scatters them so the surface stays non-directional, as in the lecture's spot designs.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions across the lecture: combining repeats, counting shared healds, two-step face proportions and the mistakes students make most.

questions.q: A student tries to superimpose an 8-end sateen and a 6-end sateen on an 8 × 8 repeat. What is the smallest repeat that actually works?
questions.explain: The lowest common multiple of 8 and 6 is 24, so the 6-end sateen will not close on 8 ends. 48 is the product, not the LCM.

questions.q: A 4-end satinette is superimposed on an 8 × 8 repeat. How many marks does the satinette alone contribute?
questions.explain: The satinette fits 2 × 2 = 4 times in the repeat, each copy with 4 single lifts: 4 × 4 = 16 marks.

questions.q: A student says the 8-end honeycomb needs 8 healds because it repeats on 8 ends. What is wrong?
options: It needs 4 healds like a 2/2 twill
The draft is pointed, so ends 6, 7, 8 share healds 4, 3, 2 and only 5 healds are needed
Nothing: healds always equal the repeat
It needs 16 healds because the lifting plan is also pointed
questions.explain: Healds are set by distinct end movements. In the pointed draft 1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2 the descending ends repeat the movements of ascending ones, so 5 frames suffice.

questions.q: One mark is added to every base mark of the irregular 6-end sateen. What percentage of the 6 × 6 repeat is filled? Give one decimal place.
questions.explain: 6 base marks + 6 added = 12 of 36 squares: 12 ÷ 36 = 0.333, i.e. 33.3 %.

questions.q: Superimposing two sateens always doubles the number of marks in the repeat.
questions.explain: Where a mark of one sateen falls on a mark of the other, the two coincide and count once, so the total can be less than the sum of the two sets.

questions.q: Why is an 8-end sateen base, left as it is, a poor crepe?
options: Because with only one mark per end it is simply a smooth sateen, not a pebbled surface; the extra marks create the texture
Because it shows a twill line
Because its repeat is too small
Because it has too many healds
questions.explain: A sateen is smooth and weft-faced. The crepe texture comes from the groups of marks added to the base, which break the surface into a pebble.

questions.q: In the honeycomb draft 1 2 3 4 5 4 3 2, ends 2 and 8 share heald 2. Which other pair of ends shares a heald?
questions.explain: End 3 and end 7 are both on heald 3 (and ends 4 and 6 on heald 4). Ends 1 and 5 are the turning points and each has a heald to itself.

questions.q: Using the lecture's pointed-draft pattern, how many healds would a 20-end honeycomb need?
questions.explain: Climb to the turning heald and return: 20 ÷ 2 + 1 = 11 healds for a 20-end repeat.

questions.q: A crepe on an 8-end sateen base carries three marks per end, so 37.5 % of its face is warp. What percentage of its BACK is warp?
questions.explain: Wherever the face shows weft the back shows warp: 100 − 37.5 = 62.5 % warp on the back.

questions.q: Two towels are woven, one in 8-end and one in 16-end honeycomb, from the same yarns. Which statement is correct?
options: They are the same ordinary honeycomb; the 16-end has larger cells, longer floats and needs 9 healds instead of 5
They are different weaves with different cell shapes
questions.explain: The lecture describes the 16-end version as the same weave on a larger cell. The only differences are the cell size, float length and the 9-heald draft.
